summary.text: Take the counterexample \(n=736>599\). If a nondecreasing representation by at most four squares had least base at least \(8\), all bases would lie between \(8\) and \(27\); elementary size bounds further reduce each of the four possible tuple lengths to finite ranges, and exhaustive checks find no tuple summing to \(736\), so \(a(736)\le 7\).

full_proof.text:
Let an admissible representation of a positive integer \(n\) mean an expression
\[
n=b_1^2+\cdots+b_r^2,
\qquad 1\le r\le 4,
\qquad 0<b_1\le b_2\le\cdots\le b_r,
\]
with integer bases. In such a representation \(b_1\) is the least base. Thus \(a(n)\) is the largest integer that occurs as \(b_1\) in an admissible representation of \(n\).

We disprove the conjecture using
\[
n=736.
\]
Certainly \(736>599\). We will prove that no admissible representation of \(736\) can have least base greater than \(7\). This will imply \(a(736)\le 7\), contrary to the conjectured conclusion \(a(736)>7\).

First, admissible representations of \(736\) do exist; for example,
\[
736=4^2+12^2+24^2=16+144+576.
\]
Thus the set whose maximum defines \(a(736)\) is nonempty. It is also finite, since every base in a representation is at most \(\lfloor\sqrt{736}\rfloor=27\). Hence it is legitimate to discuss its largest member.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there is an admissible representation whose least base is greater than \(7\). Write it as
\[
736=b_1^2+\cdots+b_r^2,
\qquad 1\le r\le4,
\qquad 8\le b_1\le\cdots\le b_r.
\]
In particular, every \(b_i\) is at least \(8\).

We first use congruences to show that every \(b_i\) must be divisible by \(4\). For the congruence argument only, pad the displayed sum with \(4-r\) zero squares, obtaining four integers \(c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4\), the nonzero ones being the \(b_i\), such that
\[
c_1^2+c_2^2+c_3^2+c_4^2=736.
\]
The zero terms are merely bookkeeping for the modular argument and are not being asserted to be part of an admissible representation.

Because \(736\equiv0\pmod4\), the number of odd \(c_i\) must be divisible by \(4\): an odd square is \(1\pmod4\), while an even square is \(0\pmod4\). With four terms, the number of odd terms is therefore either zero or four. It cannot be four, because every odd square is \(1\pmod8\), in which case the sum of the four squares would be \(4\pmod8\), whereas
\[
736\equiv0\pmod8.
\]
Consequently all four \(c_i\), and hence all the original \(b_i\), are even.

For an even integer \(c\), its square is congruent modulo \(16\) either to \(0\), if \(4\mid c\), or to \(4\), if \(c\equiv2\pmod4\). Let \(m\) be the number of the four padded terms that are congruent to \(2\pmod4\). Since
\[
736\equiv0\pmod{16},
\]
we have \(4m\equiv0\pmod{16}\). As \(0\le m\le4\), this says that either \(m=0\) or \(m=4\).

If the original representation has fewer than four terms, at least one padded term is zero, hence divisible by \(4\); therefore \(m\ne4\), and so \(m=0\). In that case all the original bases are divisible by \(4\).

It remains to consider the possibility that the original representation has exactly four terms and all four bases are congruent to \(2\pmod4\). In that case write
\[
b_i=2u_i
\]
with each \(u_i\) odd. Dividing the equality \(b_1^2+b_2^2+b_3^2+b_4^2=736\) by \(4\) gives
\[
u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2+u_4^2=184.
\]
Each odd square is \(1\pmod8\), so the left side is \(4\pmod8\). But \(184\equiv0\pmod8\), a contradiction. Thus this alternative is impossible as well.

We have proved in every case that
\[
4\mid b_i\qquad(1\le i\le r).
\]
Put \(b_i=4q_i\). Dividing the original equation by \(16\) yields
\[
46=q_1^2+\cdots+q_r^2.
\]
Since every \(b_i\ge8\), every \(q_i\ge2\). Also every individual square is at most \(46\), so \(q_i\le\lfloor\sqrt{46}\rfloor=6\). Hence each \(q_i\) belongs to the very small set
\[
\{2,3,4,5,6\}.
\]
Their squares and their residues modulo \(8\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
q&2&3&4&5&6\\ \hline
q^2&4&9&16&25&36\\
q^2\bmod8&4&1&0&1&4.
\end{array}
\]
We now exhaust the four possible values of \(r\). Notice that \(46\equiv6\pmod8\).

If \(r=1\), then \(46\) would be a square. This is impossible either from \(6^2<46<7^2\), or because a square modulo \(8\) can only be \(0,1\), or \(4\), never \(6\).

If \(r=2\), the two square residues would each lie in \(\{0,1,4\}\). The possible sums of two such residues modulo \(8\) are \(0,1,2,4,5\), never \(6\). Thus two squares cannot sum to \(46\).

Suppose \(r=3\). The only multiset of three residues selected from \(\{0,1,4\}\) whose sum is \(6\pmod8\) is
\[
\{1,1,4\}.
\]
Indeed, without a residue \(4\), three residues \(0\) or \(1\) sum to at most \(3\); with one residue \(4\), the other two must both be \(1\); and two or three residues \(4\) cannot give residue \(6\) after adding the remaining residue.

According to the table, the two residue-\(1\) bases must each be either \(3\) or \(5\), while the residue-\(4\) base must be either \(2\) or \(6\). The sum of the two residue-\(1\) squares can therefore only be
\[
3^2+3^2=18,\qquad 3^2+5^2=34,\qquad 5^2+5^2=50.
\]
If the remaining base is \(2\), the total is respectively
\[
22,\quad38,\quad54;
\]
if it is \(6\), the total is respectively
\[
54,\quad70,\quad86.
\]
None is \(46\). Thus \(r=3\) is impossible.

Finally suppose \(r=4\). The only multiset of four residues from \(\{0,1,4\}\) whose sum is \(6\pmod8\) is
\[
\{0,1,1,4\}.
\]
To see this directly, let \(s\) be the number of residue-\(1\) terms and \(t\) the number of residue-\(4\) terms. Then \(s+t\le4\), and the sum is congruent to \(s+4t\pmod8\). If \(t=0\), this is at most \(4\). If \(t=1\), congruence to \(6\) forces \(s=2\), leaving one residue-\(0\) term. If \(t=2\), the residue is \(s\) and cannot be \(6\), since \(s\le2\). If \(t=3\), the residue is \(4+s\), with \(s\le1\), and if \(t=4\), it is \(0\). Thus precisely the pattern \(\{0,1,1,4\}\) can occur.

Within \(\{2,3,4,5,6\}\), the unique base whose square is \(0\pmod8\) is \(4\); the two residue-\(1\) bases are each \(3\) or \(5\); and the residue-\(4\) base is \(2\) or \(6\). The fixed residue-\(0\) square contributes \(4^2=16\), while the pair of residue-\(1\) squares contributes one of \(18,34,50\), as above. If the residue-\(4\) base is \(2\), the possible totals are
\[
16+4+18=38,
\qquad16+4+34=54,
\qquad16+4+50=70.
\]
If that base is \(6\), the possible totals are
\[
16+36+18=70,
\qquad16+36+34=86,
\qquad16+36+50=102.
\]
Again none is \(46\). Thus \(r=4\) is impossible.

All possibilities \(1\le r\le4\) have now been eliminated. Therefore \(736\) has no admissible representation all of whose bases are at least \(8\). In particular, no integer \(k>7\) can occur as the least base of an admissible representation of \(736\): if the least base were \(k>7\), nondecreasing order would force every base to be at least \(8\), exactly the situation just proved impossible.

It follows that every candidate in the maximum defining \(a(736)\) is at most \(7\), and hence
\[
a(736)\le7.
\]
Since \(736>599\), this single value contradicts the assertion that \(a(n)>7\) for every integer \(n>599\). Consequently
\[
\neg\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb N,\;599<n\Longrightarrow a(n)>7\bigr),
\]
which is the desired disproof.
